period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 9 periods = 360 minutes
Total: 9 periods · 6h 0min

periods.activity_title: Incredible India: Reading the Introductory Passage Aloud

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.131): five questions on Hamara Bharat passage.

time_bands.activity: Open the chapter at page 131. Read 'Hamara Bharat — Incredible India!' aloud, pausing at key phrases — wise people, unity in diversity, rivers and mountains — so students follow in their books.
Revisit the passage together. Ask students what Bharat is known for, what makes it attractive, and which geographical features are mentioned, drawing answers from the text on page 131.

Take the deeper questions from 'Let us discuss' (p.131): why living in unison is special, and what advice the passage gives. Invite two or three students to respond in full sentences; affirm and extend each answer.
Close with a quick pair-share: each pair names one thing from the passage that surprised them about Bharat. Take two responses aloud.

periods.teacher_notes: This is the chapter's opening informational text, which sets up the unity-in-diversity theme that runs through every art form described later. Students may answer in single words at first — nudge them toward complete sentences using the passage's own language. The vocabulary fill-in activity on page 132 (folk art, culture, festivals, languages) has not been done in class and is a useful independent reading exercise students may explore on their own.

periods.activity_title: The Video Conference Begins: Aipan and Dhokra

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.133): two questions on the Ek Bharat programme.
Let us discuss (p.136): complete the table for Aipan and Dhokra.

time_bands.activity: Read Part I of the main text (p.133) together — the video conference opening and Aakansha's description of Aipan — with teacher and students sharing sentences. Pause to name the key materials: rice flour paste, geru, geometric designs.

Take the two 'Let us discuss' questions (p.133): what the Ek Bharat, Shreshtha Bharat programme is about and why it is conducted. Students respond briefly; teacher fills in context from the informational note.

Continue shared reading through Priyaranjan's description of Dhokra (p.133–135). Pause at the lost-wax process — clay, wax carving, firing, molten brass — and invite students to visualise each step before reading the next.
Students begin filling in the table on page 136 for Aakansha (Aipan) and Priyaranjan (Dhokra) using the text just read. Pairs compare their entries; teacher reviews correct answers aloud.

periods.teacher_notes: The lost-wax (cire perdue) process is the most conceptually complex art form in the text — students often confuse the role of wax and brass. A quick gesture sequence (coat → carve → cover → fire → pour) helps fix the order. The vocabulary fill-in activity on page 132 remains unanchored in class and can serve as independent reading.

periods.activity_title: Coconut Shell Craft and Kondapalli Toys: Completing the Picture

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.136): complete table rows for Kerala and Andhra Pradesh.
Let us think and reflect — I (p.136): four fill-in-the-blank sentences.

homework.task_brief: Let us think and reflect — II, III, IV (p.136): three short-answer questions on Aipan, Dhokra, and Kondapalli.

time_bands.activity: Read Chitra's description of coconut shell craft (p.135–136) together, then Balamurali's account of Kondapalli toy-making. Students listen and annotate key materials and steps in their books.
Students complete the remaining two rows of the table on page 136 (Chitra — Kerala; Balamurali — Andhra Pradesh) individually. Take answers aloud and correct any gaps about makku or wood polish.

Work through the four fill-in-the-blank sentences from 'Let us think and reflect — I' (p.136) as a class. Read each stem, give thinking time, then nominate students for the answer — affirm using the text.

Introduce the homework: three reflective questions from 'Let us think and reflect — II, III, IV' (p.136). Read the questions aloud together so students understand what is being asked before they write.

periods.teacher_notes: Having read the descriptions of all four art forms, students can now see the full table as a comparative overview of craft traditions across India. A common slip is confusing makku (tamarind seed powder + sawdust paste) with the wood itself — the text is precise about its role as a joining agent. The three deeper comprehension questions set for homework ask students to reason from the text, not simply recall.

periods.activity_title: Gakkad Bharta: Listening to a Food Description from Madhya Pradesh

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us listen (p.138): complete speaker notes from gakkad bharta description.
Let us listen (p.138): complete the step-by-step flowchart for gakkad bharta.

time_bands.activity: Briefly orient students: they are about to hear a speaker from Jabalpur, Madhya Pradesh describe a traditional dish. Ask them to have their books open at page 138 and read the note-completion frame before listening.
Read the transcript aloud at a measured pace as Sushil's voice. Students complete the five speaker-notes blanks on page 138 (name, town, state, food item, vegetables). Pause after each natural chunk.
Check the five notes answers together. Clarify 'Jabalpur' and 'Madhya Pradesh' for any student who missed them, and confirm 'brinjal and tomatoes' as the vegetables roasted for bharta.
Read the transcript a second time, more slowly. Students now complete the three-step flowchart on page 138 — wheat dough balls roasted, bharta garnished, gakkad crumbled and served with ghee.
Take the flowchart answers aloud, step by step. Students self-correct. Ask: 'What makes gakkad bharta different from fried food?' — a brief class response drawn from the transcript.

periods.teacher_notes: The transcript is Sushil's first-person description of gakkad bharta, a dish from Jabalpur; it extends the chapter's cultural-diversity theme from craft to food. Students often miss 'Jabalpur' as distinct from the state 'Madhya Pradesh' — reading the frame before the first listen helps. The second listen is deliberately slower; use natural sentence boundaries as pauses rather than reading at conversation speed.

periods.activity_title: My Region's Art Form: Structured Oral Presentations

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us speak (p.138): present a local art form using given sentence starters.

time_bands.activity: Remind students of the four children in the text — Aakansha, Priyaranjan, Chitra, Balamurali — and the structure each used: name the art form, list materials, explain the process. Display the sentence starters from page 138 on the board.

Students choose an art form from their own region — painting, rangoli, metal craft, embroidery, music, dance, or drama — and prepare a brief oral presentation using the starter phrases and sequence words from page 138. Allow quiet individual thinking and note-making.

Five or six students present to the class, each for about two to three minutes. The class listens actively and may ask one clarifying question after each presentation. Teacher notes fluency and use of sequence words.

Brief class reflection: which presentation taught the class something new? Take two or three responses. Affirm correct use of 'first', 'after that', 'finally' and similar sequence words from the chapter.

periods.teacher_notes: Having heard the four video-conference descriptions in the main text, students now produce a parallel oral act using the same structure. Encourage hesitant speakers to use the starter phrases as a scaffold — 'I know about the art form called…' reduces the anxiety of beginning. Students who cannot name a local art form may describe a familiar activity such as rangoli or a festival food-making tradition.
materials: English textbook, p.138; board or display for sentence starters

periods.activity_title: Sequence Words and Present-Tense Agreement in Context

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.137): fill sequence words into 'How I Get Ready for School'.
Let us learn (p.137): make five sentences using pronouns, verbs, and -s/-es.

time_bands.activity: Open the chapter at page 137. Revisit the sequence words used by Priyaranjan, Chitra, and Balamurali — 'to begin, first, then, after that, next, finally, at last' — by quickly recalling one step of the Dhokra process that used each word.

Students complete the 'How I Get Ready for School' paragraph (p.137) individually, using each sequence word only once. Pairs compare answers; teacher takes responses aloud and confirms the correct order.

Introduce the subject-verb agreement task (p.137). Explain that in the text the children use first-person and third-person verbs — 'I draw' versus 'she draws'. Students make five sentences from the word table, adding -s/-es where needed.
Three or four students read their sentences aloud. Class identifies whether -s/-es was applied correctly. Teacher addresses the two examples from the textbook to model the pattern before closing.

periods.teacher_notes: The sequence words arise directly from how the art-making processes are described in the main text, so students have a meaningful context for each word. The most common error in the subject-verb agreement task is omitting -s/-es with 'he/she/it' for irregular-seeming verbs like 'practise' and 'speak' — brief board work on these two may prevent the error.
materials: English textbook, p.137; board for -s/-es examples

periods.activity_title: My Favourite Art Form: Planning, Drafting, and Sharing a Paragraph

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write (p.139): write a five-sentence paragraph on the most-liked art form.

time_bands.activity: Pairs discuss briefly which of the four art forms — Aipan, Dhokra, coconut shell craft, or Kondapalli toys — they liked most and why. Teacher takes two or three spoken responses to model the reasoning students should use in writing.

Teacher models a five-sentence paragraph plan on the board: sentence 1 — name the art form and state; sentences 2–4 — three reasons using evidence from the text; sentence 5 — a personal reflection. Students jot their own plan.

Students write their paragraph independently (p.139 task). Teacher circulates, prompting those who give only one reason to look back at the relevant section of the main text for a second or third detail.
Peer response: students exchange books and read their partner's paragraph. The reader underlines one sentence they think is the strongest reason and writes one word of feedback at the margin.

Two or three students read their paragraphs aloud. Brief class comment on whether five sentences were used and whether reasons were drawn from the text. Teacher names one specific strength from each reading.

periods.teacher_notes: The paragraph task requires students to give reasons grounded in the text descriptions, not simply state a preference — circulating during drafting to check this is important. A five-sentence structure is an explicit requirement of the task, so the modelled plan on the board keeps students on track. Both drafting and peer response are completed within this unit so no written work carries over.
materials: English textbook, p.135–139; board for paragraph plan model

periods.activity_title: Madhubani Colours and Ek Bharat Pairing: Exploring Beyond the Text

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us explore (p.139): prepare natural colours and apply to Madhubani outline.
Let us explore (p.140): find your state's Ek Bharat pairing and discuss cultural interests.

time_bands.activity: Briefly introduce Madhubani painting from Bihar (p.139): artists use natural colours on house walls. Read aloud the five colour sources — haldi (yellow), leaves (green), geru (red), flowers (orange), neel (blue).

Students colour the Madhubani painting outline on page 139 using natural-colour materials brought to class or available crayons representing the natural colours. Teacher circulates to ask which colour source each student is using.

Read the Ek Bharat, Shreshtha Bharat informational note (p.140) together. Students discuss in pairs: which state theirs is paired with, and one cultural practice from that state they would like to learn about.

Three pairs share their state-pairing findings aloud. Close by connecting back to the chapter's theme: four art forms from four states — now each student's state-pair adds another layer to India's cultural map.

periods.teacher_notes: The Madhubani activity extends the chapter's craft theme into a hands-on experience — students who have only watercolour pencils can still participate by labelling their colours with their natural source names. The Ek Bharat state-pairing activity works even if students are unsure of their exact pairing; the discussion of what they would want to learn is the substantive part. Both activities are completed within this unit.
materials: English textbook, p.139–140; natural colouring materials (haldi, leaves, flower petals, geru powder, neel) or crayons; Madhubani outline on p.139

periods.activity_title: Unity in Diversity: Bringing the Whole Chapter Together

time_bands.activity: Open with a whole-class recall: teacher names one art form — Aipan, Dhokra, coconut shell craft, Kondapalli — and students call out the state, material, and one key step. This surfaces what the chapter taught across all four traditions.

Critical discussion: what do Aipan, Dhokra, coconut shell craft, and Kondapalli have in common beyond being art forms? Guide students toward ideas of community transmission, natural materials, and cultural identity without telling them the answers.

Students write four to five sentences independently: 'What does unity in diversity mean to me, based on what the children in the video conference shared?' They must name at least two art forms and use at least two sequence words from the chapter in their response.

Three students read their sentences aloud. Class gives a quick thumbs-up for each sequence word used correctly. Teacher closes by affirming the Ek Bharat, Shreshtha Bharat spirit as the chapter's central idea.

periods.teacher_notes: This synthesis draws on the content of all four art-form descriptions and the informational note on the Ek Bharat programme. The writing task is a new, self-contained prompt — students choose their own angle and evidence from what the chapter taught, completing the piece within this unit. The grammar constraint (sequence words) is a natural application of the vocabulary_grammar work in the chapter.
materials: English textbook, p.131–140; board for recall list

items.item_stem:
Read the following statements about the art forms described in 'Kalakritiyon ka Bharat'. Write True or False for each statement.
1. Aipan designs are made using white rice flour paste applied on brick-red walls and floors.
2. The Dhokra metal craft tradition is approximately 400 years old.
3. Coconut shell craft in Kerala produces household items such as bowls and jewellery.
4. Kondapalli toys are joined using a paste made from tamarind seed powder and sawdust.

options.text: Aipan designs are made using white rice flour paste applied on brick-red walls and floors.
The Dhokra metal craft tradition is approximately 400 years old.
Coconut shell craft in Kerala produces household items such as bowls and jewellery.
Kondapalli toys are joined using a paste made from tamarind seed powder and sawdust.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer:
1. True — rice flour paste on geru (brick-red) surfaces is the defining technique of Aipan.
2. False — Dhokra is described as 4,000 years old, not 400.
3. True — the text lists bowls and jewellery as products of coconut shell craft.
4. True — makku is explicitly described as tamarind seed powder mixed with sawdust.

items.item_stem: The Ek Bharat, Shreshtha Bharat programme brings together children from different states to share their traditional art forms. Based on the descriptions given by Aakansha, Priyaranjan, Chitra, and Balamurali, what do you think is the most important reason for preserving traditional art forms? Support your answer with at least one specific detail from the text.

expected_elements: Identifies a reason — cultural identity, heritage, or community tradition.
Supports with a specific art form detail from the text.
Shows understanding that art forms carry regional identity.
Written in complete sentences.

items.item_stem:
Listen to Sushil's description of gakkad bharta (p.162) and fill in the blanks.
1. Sushil is from ___________, which is in the state of ___________.
2. To make gakkad, balls of ___________ dough are roasted on ___________ heat.
3. The vegetable roasted to make bharta are ___________ and ___________.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1. Jabalpur; Madhya Pradesh. 2. wheat; high. 3. brinjals (brinjal); tomatoes.

Describes gakkad (wheat balls roasted) and bharta (brinjal and tomatoes roasted, garnished).
Notes the serving method: crumble gakkad, add bharta and ghee.
Connects pride to the dish's uniqueness or regional identity.

items.item_stem: Imagine you are a participant in the Ek Bharat, Shreshtha Bharat video conference. In two to three minutes, tell the class about a traditional art form or food from your region. expected_elements: Names a specific regional art form or food clearly.
Lists at least two materials or ingredients.
Uses at least two sequence words to order the steps.

items.item_stem: In the video conference, children from four different states discovered that their art forms — though very different — share some common values. In a short role-play with a partner, one of you plays a student from Uttarakhand (Aipan) and the other plays a student from Odisha (Dhokra). Discuss what your two art forms have in common and why it matters to keep them alive. Each speaker should give at least one reason.

expected_elements: Each speaker stays in role and names their art form accurately.
At least one common feature identified (e.g., natural materials, community tradition).
Both speakers give a reason for preserving the art form.
Exchange is conversational and uses complete sentences.

Write a short paragraph (four to six sentences) in which you imagine you are one of those children. Explain your art form to a friend who has never heard of it, and say why you think people should keep making it.

expected_elements: Writes clearly in the first person as one of the four children.
Describes the art form accurately using at least one process detail.

Uses imaginative or persuasive language appropriate to the audience.

items.item_stem: Match each sequence word in Column A with the sentence part in Column B that best completes the description of how Priyaranjan makes a Dhokra figure.
items.visual_stimulus:
Column A | Column B
First | the craftsperson coats a clay figure with a layer of wax.
After that | fine details of the design are carved into the wax.
Next | the wax-coated figure is covered with more clay and fired.
Then | molten brass is poured in through small openings.
Finally | the outer clay layer is removed to reveal the brass figure.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: First — the craftsperson coats a clay figure with a layer of wax; After that — fine details of the design are carved into the wax; Next — the wax-coated figure is covered with more clay and fired; Then — molten brass is poured in through small openings; Finally — the outer clay layer is removed to reveal the brass figure.

answer_key.right: the craftsperson coats a clay figure with a layer of wax.
fine details of the design are carved into the wax.
the wax-coated figure is covered with more clay and fired.
molten brass is poured in through small openings.
the outer clay layer is removed to reveal the brass figure.

items.item_stem:
Each sentence below describes what one of the children in the video conference does. Choose the correct verb form (given in brackets) to complete each sentence, then write the complete sentence.
1. Aakansha (draw / draws) Aipan patterns on the floor every festival.
2. Priyaranjan (explain / explains) how wax melts when the clay figure is fired.
3. Chitra and Balamurali (describe / describes) craft traditions from their states.
4. Balamurali (use / uses) makku to join the carved wooden pieces together.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1. Aakansha draws Aipan patterns on the floor every festival. 2. Priyaranjan explains how wax melts when the clay figure is fired. 3. Chitra and Balamurali describe craft traditions from their states. 4. Balamurali uses makku to join the carved wooden pieces together.

items.item_stem: The chapter tells you that Madhubani artists from Bihar use natural colours such as haldi (yellow), geru (red), and neel (blue) to paint on the walls of their houses. Using any two of these natural colour sources, create a simple pattern inspired by the Madhubani tradition. On the same page, write two sentences explaining which colours you used and where each colour comes from.

expected_elements: Pattern reflects at least one Madhubani-inspired element (geometric or nature motif).
Two natural colour sources are named correctly (haldi, geru, neel, leaves, or flowers).
Two sentences correctly state the source of each colour.
Work shows engagement with the chapter's cultural theme.

items.item_stem: The Ek Bharat, Shreshtha Bharat programme pairs each state with another state to promote cultural exchange and unity. Find out which state your state is paired with. Then prepare a short illustrated or written report (one page) that includes: the name of your paired state, one traditional art form or cultural practice from that state, one thing you would like to learn or try from that state's culture, and why cultural exchange between states is important.

expected_elements: Correctly names the student's state-pair under the programme.
Identifies a specific art form or cultural practice from the paired state.
Explains a personal learning interest with a clear reason.
Connects the activity to the chapter's unity-in-diversity theme.
